strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: building multimodal interactive systems without costly end-to-end multimodal training. The modular orchestration framing, with a controller LLM, specialized expert models, shared memory, and TTS streaming, is a reasonable systems direction.

The proposed components are intuitively useful for deployment: explicit control tokens can improve interpretability, the memory pool could avoid repeated modality calls in multi-turn interactions, and parallel TTS chunking addresses a real latency bottleneck.

The manuscript attempts broad empirical coverage across multimodal understanding, video, OCR, diagram, math, and TTS latency benchmarks, which is the right evaluation scope for the claimed omni-modal orchestration system.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not convincingly supported. The system appears to route among strong existing expert models, especially Qwen2.5-VL variants, but the comparisons are presented as if the orchestration method itself outperforms trained omni-models. This is not an apples-to-apples evaluation, and improvements may simply come from selecting stronger back-end models rather than from the proposed orchestration.

The experimental protocol is underspecified. The paper does not clearly describe routing policies, prompts used in evaluation, benchmark-specific settings, whether test sets are public/held out, how official results were mixed with newly run results, or how response-time measurements were collected. The statement that some results are referenced from official papers further weakens comparability.

There are no convincing ablations isolating the contributions of the controller, cross-modal memory, routing, ASR integration, or parallel TTS. Claims such as memory improving complex visual tasks and controller-based fusion improving video understanding are asserted without controlled experiments against simple baselines.

The method is mostly high-level system description rather than a technically precise contribution. Important functions such as semantic classification, memory retrieval, compression, integration, prosodic adjustment, and interruption detection are defined abstractly but not specified enough for implementation or analysis.

Reproducibility is poor: no code, no exact model versions/checkpoints, no inference parameters, no routing logs, no benchmark scripts, no hardware details, and no statistical uncertainty are provided. The appendix gives only schematic pseudocode and prompt fragments.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations or ethics discussion, despite deploying multimodal memory, audio interaction, ASR/TTS, and potentially user data storage. Privacy, consent, failure modes, safety of tool/model routing, and risks from retaining multimodal data are not addressed.

Presentation quality is below the expected standard. Several figures/tables render with garbled text or extraction artifacts, there are many typos and spacing issues, and some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, for example describing the approach as superior to commercial systems while relying on heterogeneous external experts.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: building multimodal interactive systems without costly end-to-end retraining, which is important for extensibility and deployment.

The proposed high-level architecture is easy to understand: a controller LLM emits routing/control tokens, invokes specialized models, stores cross-modal memory, and streams responses through segmented parallel TTS.
The modular framing could be useful as an engineering pattern, especially for rapidly combining stronger off-the-shelf vision, audio, reasoning, and TTS components.
weaknesses: The central technical contribution is weakly substantiated. The controller-token orchestration, JSON memory pool, and parallel TTS segmentation are described mostly at the level of prompts, schemas, and simple workflow logic, without enough algorithmic novelty or rigorous design detail for a main-track ML contribution.

The experimental methodology is not reliable. The paper states that some baseline results are taken from official papers, while the proposed system combines multiple specialized models. This makes comparisons to single models such as GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-Omni, VITA, and Qwen2.5-VL difficult to interpret and likely unfair unless inference budgets, model access, prompting, ensembling policy, and benchmark protocols are carefully controlled, which they are not.

Claims of outperforming state-of-the-art models are not adequately supported. For example, the paper reports large gains on MMBench, MMStar, MMMU, MathVision, and other benchmarks, but does not provide enough information about routing decisions, prompts, number of calls, answer extraction, benchmark versions, evaluation scripts, or whether test leakage/benchmark contamination was considered.

The claimed benefits of the cross-modal memory system are not convincingly evaluated. The manuscript asserts that memory improves context-aware visual tasks, but does not present controlled ablations isolating memory from stronger expert-model selection, prompt effects, ASR-derived text, or repeated model calls.

The TTS contribution is minor and under-evaluated. A 10.3% latency reduction from segment-level parallelism is plausible but modest, and the paper does not provide enough details on hardware, TTS model, text lengths, concurrency settings, quality metrics, user studies, or boundary artifacts to support claims about naturalness and full-duplex interaction.

Reproducibility is poor. The manuscript lacks released code details, complete prompts beyond a simplified appendix template, concrete routing rules, model versions/API settings, hardware, latency measurement protocol, random seeds where applicable, full benchmark commands, and ablation configurations.

Presentation quality is below the expected standard. The writing contains many grammatical issues, formatting problems, inconsistent terminology, and corrupted/extracted figure text; several figures and tables are hard to interpret. The paper also overclaims, using phrases such as 'consistently outperforms all competitors' despite mixed results and unclear comparisons.

The related-work positioning is incomplete. Agent/tool orchestration for multimodal systems is already a common paradigm, and the paper does not clearly distinguish its contribution from existing tool-using multimodal agents beyond applying the idea to a particular system stack.

Limitations and ethics are essentially missing. For a system integrating speech, vision, memory, and external models, the paper should discuss privacy, consent, data retention, safety in audio/visual interactions, benchmark contamination, model licensing, and risks from routing or memory errors.
Overall, the work may be a useful prototype or demo paper, but the evidence, reproducibility, and technical depth are insufficient for ICML main-track acceptance.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical problem: building multimodal interactive systems without costly joint training. The orchestration framing is timely and useful for real deployments where modularity, model replacement, and interpretability matter.

The proposed architecture is easy to understand: a controller LLM emits explicit routing/control tokens, expert models handle modality-specific work, a JSON-like memory pool carries context, and parallel TTS reduces perceived latency. This makes the system conceptually extensible and inspectable.

The experimental section covers a broad range of benchmarks, including MMBench, MMStar, Video-MME, MMMU, MathVision, CC-OCR, AI2D, and InfoVQA. The reported numbers suggest that model orchestration can be competitive with trained omni-modal systems, which is a promising empirical direction.
The paper includes useful implementation-level details in the appendix, such as the controller prompt format, instruction tokens, memory schema, algorithm sketch, and TTS segmentation rules.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is not yet soundly supported. The system appears to combine multiple strong specialist models, including Qwen2.5-VL variants and other executors, while many baselines are single models and some baseline numbers are taken from official papers. Without controlled, same-backbone, same-budget comparisons, it is hard to attribute gains to the proposed orchestration rather than model selection or benchmark reporting differences.

The method is underspecified in several decisive places. The paper does not give enough detail on routing decisions, expert selection, semantic classification, memory retrieval, compression, prompt construction, failure handling, or how benchmark answers are produced when multiple experts are available. This substantially weakens reproducibility.

There are few ablations. The paper should isolate the contribution of the controller, cross-modal memory, expert routing, ASR/text fusion, and TTS batching. Claims such as memory improving complex visual tasks and controller-based fusion improving video understanding are plausible but not directly tested against strong ablated variants.

The latency and efficiency claims are incomplete. The paper reports a response-time column and a 10.3% TTS improvement, but does not provide hardware, serving setup, model-call counts, concurrency assumptions, end-to-end latency distribution, cost, or comparison under matched compute. A multi-model orchestrator may be more expensive than a single omni model even if perceived TTS latency improves.

The work does not convincingly evaluate the interactive/full-duplex aspects that motivate the paper. There is no user study or systematic benchmark for interruption handling, natural conversational flow, speech quality, cross-turn multimodal consistency, or real-time behavior under streaming inputs.

Originality is moderate rather than high. Controller-token routing, tool/model orchestration, memory pools, and streaming chunked TTS are established ideas in agent systems. The contribution is mostly an integration and application to MLLMs; that can be useful, but the paper should position itself more carefully against existing multimodal agents and tool-use systems.

Presentation and polish need improvement. Some sections contain grammatical errors, formatting problems, repeated claims, and at least one figure appears partially cut off. The paper also overstates results, e.g. describing broad superiority over commercial systems despite GPT-4o leading on Video-MME and despite uncontrolled comparisons.

Limitations, ethics, and privacy are underdeveloped. A cross-modal memory pool storing audio, visual, and dialogue context raises privacy and data-retention concerns, and the framework depends on potentially proprietary or opaque expert models. These issues should be discussed explicitly, along with failure modes from incorrect routing, hallucinated memory summaries, and modality-specific bias.
